source: Hu, Storks, Lewis, Chai (2023) In-Context Analogical Reasoning with Pre-Trained Language Models
finding: Tests the Gentner/Christie idea directly: turn RAVEN matrices into text by NAMING entity attributes (type, size, color) as ordinal symbols. Naming the attributes lets a plain language model solve visual matrix analogies zero-shot.
numbers: RAVEN Center sub-task, GPT-3 175B: 77.2% with entity naming, near human level. Quasi-image ASCII encoding reached only up to 28.2%. Random-word naming up to 51.8%. Ordinal naming beat random naming by over 20 points at larger sizes.
quote: assigning even nonsensical names to relations enhances children's relational reasoning
limits: Names helped most when they carried usable order (numbers). Not a test of children. Naming was done by the authors' mapping, not by the model.
agent_relevance: Supports S2 (name the relation or attribute before comparing). Name choice matters: names that encode order beat arbitrary names.

source: Hu et al. (2023) In-Context Analogical Reasoning, decomposition result
finding: Splitting the problem into separate prompts per attribute (decomposition) adds more gains, and helps small models most.
numbers: Center: +2.8 points for GPT-3 175B; OPT 125M doubled from 22.2% to 45.6%; OPT 1.3B rose 47.2% to 72.0%. 3x3Grid: 86.4% to 93.2%, above humans. Component decomposition alone gave about +20 points on multi-component tasks; OPT 1.3B went from 20-30% to over 70%.
limits: Zero-shot, one benchmark family. Decomposition and naming are confounded in some rows.
agent_relevance: Name-then-compare, one attribute at a time, is a cheap scaffold; weaker sub-agents gain the most.

source: Hu et al. (2023) robustness of naming to distractors
finding: Adding a distracting attribute (orientation) with RAVEN values or random values barely hurt the named-attribute prompts.
numbers: Center accuracy 76.0% and 80.0% with RAVEN orientation values (two settings), 72.6% and 77.8% with random values.
limits: Only one distractor type tested.
agent_relevance: Named structured fields let the model ignore irrelevant attributes.

source: Hu et al. (2023) comparison to supervised baselines
finding: With full naming plus decomposition, a zero-shot LM matches or beats trained vision models on several RAVEN sub-tasks.
numbers: L-R 77.6%, U-D 78.0%, O-IC 82.8%, O-IG 92.6% for GPT-3 175B; exceeds humans and nears supervised baselines on the last.
limits: Authors' own abstraction pipeline; RAVEN has known shortcut issues (they also test Impartial-RAVEN).
agent_relevance: A language layer over a perceptual task can replace training.

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: GPT-3 matched or beat UCLA undergraduates on text matrix, letter-string and verbal analogies, and showed human-like error patterns.
numbers: Digit Matrices (human N=40): GPT-3 above humans, generative OR=1.88 p=.005; multiple choice OR=6.27. Letter strings (N=57): GPT-3 OR=1.76, driven by zero-generalization items. Verbal analogy sets: GPT-3 at or above human average on UCLA VAT (N=57), Sternberg-Nigro (N=20), SAT problems above high-school estimate; Jones et al. set numerically weaker.
limits: Later shown not robust (see Lewis and Mitchell lines). Training-data overlap possible. Not a label manipulation.
agent_relevance: Baseline claim that relational words in text are enough for relation mapping; our agent should still test robustness.

source: Webb et al. (2023) story analogies (Gentner et al. 1993 materials)
finding: On Gentner's far story analogies GPT-3 chose the causally matching story above chance but was worse than humans; GPT-4 improved.
numbers: Human N=54: 15/54 chose the analogous story every trial. GPT-3 vs humans OR=0.37, p=.0003 (humans better). Humans t(53)=21.3 combined, 16.7 far. GPT-4 reported as nearly perfect in near and stronger in far (exact value in supplement, not read).
limits: Only 18 problems; GPT-4 tested via web interface.
agent_relevance: Relational (causal) matching beats surface matching in big models but is fragile.

source: Lewis & Mitchell (2024) Using counterfactual tasks to evaluate the generality of analogical reasoning in LLMs
finding: Letter-string analogies with permuted or symbol alphabets: humans stay high, GPT-3, GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 drop sharply. Models passed the comprehension check of the new alphabet but failed to apply the relation.
numbers: Human samples 46 per point (vs 57 in Webb). Error type 'alternate rule': 38.59% of one group's errors, 22% GPT-4, 5.81% GPT-3 (table row order read as human, GPT-4, GPT-3 from the text). GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 no better than GPT-3.
limits: Exact accuracies are in figures (not extracted). Prompt format from Hodel and West.
agent_relevance: Relation names ('successor' in a new order) do not transfer if the relation was never grounded. Test with counterfactual variants.

source: Lewis & Mitchell (2024) Evaluating the robustness of analogical reasoning in LLMs: digit matrices
finding: Digit-matrix analogies: swapping symbols did nothing, but moving the blank position collapsed GPT accuracy while humans were unaffected.
numbers: Mean accuracy Digits / Alt-Blank / Symbols as read from jumbled table: humans 0.715/0.771/0.704; GPT models 0.813/0.480/0.790 and 0.810/0.477/0.792. Samples: humans 1,550/1,000/1,000; GPT 2,916/1,466/2,100.
limits: Row labels in extracted table are scrambled, so assignment to GPT-3.5 vs GPT-4 is uncertain.
agent_relevance: Relational format changes break models more than content changes: vary layout in agent tests.

source: Lewis & Mitchell (2024) story analogies: order and paraphrase
finding: GPT-4 on Gentner's story analogies was biased by answer order and sensitive to paraphrase of the correct story; humans were not.
numbers: In Webb's data GPT-4 was 89% (16/18) when Story A was correct vs 61% (11/18) when Story B was correct. Paraphrased correct targets lowered GPT-4 more than humans (numbers in figures, not extracted).
limits: 18 items; sentence-level similarity shortcut argued by authors.
agent_relevance: Randomize option order and paraphrase before trusting relation matches.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large Language Models as Analogical Reasoners
finding: Prompt the model to recall relevant solved problems and knowledge itself before solving. Beats fixed-example CoT.
numbers: Average gain about +4% over baselines. GSM8K GPT3.5-turbo: 5-shot CoT 75.0% vs self-generated exemplars 75.8-77.8%. text-davinci-003 14.8% vs 50.3-61.0%. MATH GPT3.5: 33.0% vs 33.9-37.3%. Codeforces and BIG-Bench gains also reported.
limits: Table columns partly scrambled in text extraction; variant rows (K, knowledge) not fully mapped.
agent_relevance: Analogy as a scaffold step in an agent loop.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) prompt design: identify core concepts before exemplars
finding: The code variant asks the model to name the core concepts or algorithms first, then recall analogous problems.
numbers: K=5 exemplars for GSM8K, K=3 for MATH and BIG-Bench; Codeforces uses self-generated knowledge plus 3 exemplars.
limits: No ablation separating the concept-naming step in the parts read.
agent_relevance: Template for an S2 step: name the relation or concept, then retrieve analogs.

source: Yu, He, Ying (2024) Thought Propagation: an analogical approach to complex reasoning with LLMs
finding: Agent loop that proposes analogous problems, solves them, and reuses their solutions to fix the original answer.
numbers: Abstract: +12% absolute optimal-solution rate in shortest-path reasoning, +13% human preference in creative writing, +15% task completion in LLM-agent planning over baselines.
limits: Gains from abstract; per-model tables not extracted. Extra calls cost.
agent_relevance: Analogy retrieval inside an agent loop with a measured planning gain.

source: Stevenson et al. (2023) Do large language models solve verbal analogies like children do?
finding: Six Dutch LLMs solve children's verbal analogies mostly by association with the C term, not relation mapping.
numbers: 622 analogies solved by 14,006 children aged 7-12. Models from about 7-year-old level (M-GPT) to slightly above 11-year-old (XLM-V, GPT-3). Controlling for association drops each model 1-2 years of age level. With only the C term, about 33% (one model) and 28% (XLM-V) of items were still solved.
limits: Dutch items; older models.
agent_relevance: Include distractors that are associates of C when testing relation use.

source: Ushio et al. (2021) BERT is to NLP what AlexNet is to CV: can pre-trained LMs identify analogies?
finding: Off-the-shelf BERT, RoBERTa and GPT-2 solve word analogies to a degree but struggle with abstract relations and depend strongly on setup.
numbers: Full SAT: GPT-3 few-shot 65.2% (starred, not directly comparable), Latent Relational Analysis 56.4, FastText 49.7, GloVe 48.9, word2vec 42.8, PMI 23.3, random 20.0.
limits: Table read from text extraction; starred results tuned.
agent_relevance: Older baseline: relation words alone are not enough without a scoring design.

source: Musker, Duchnowski, Milliere, Pavlick (2025) LLMs as models for analogical reasoning
finding: Tasks map semantically meaningful words to arbitrary letter or symbol strings. GPT-4, Claude 3 and Llama-405B match humans in many conditions but differ with semantic distractors and numeric conditions.
numbers: In Defaults none of the top models differed significantly from humans (GPT-4 coef -0.77, ns). Claude 3 lower in another condition (coef -1.78, p<.001). GPT-4 fails numeric relation conditions where humans do not.
limits: Match-to-reference measure; many conditions; closed models.
agent_relevance: Re-representing words as abstract labels is a stress test for naming relations.

source: Lee et al. (2025) The Curious Case of Analogies: investigating analogical reasoning in LLMs
finding: Mechanistic study: relation info sits in mid-upper layers in correct cases; failures are missing relation info or failure to apply it to the new entity. Patching hidden states fixes some cases.
numbers: Patching recovered up to 38.4% of failed cases in one setting and up to 38.1% in another; per-model gains +32.3% (Llama-2-13B), +38.4% (Gemma-7B), +35.6% (Qwen2.5-14B).
limits: Only open 7-14B models; patching needs internals; table headers not fully read.
agent_relevance: Applying a named relation is as much a bottleneck as finding it: add an explicit apply-and-check step.

source: Liu, Marjieh, Zhu, Goldberg, Griffiths (2026) LLMs provide support for the parallelogram theory of analogy
finding: LLM-generated four-term analogies are rated better than human ones and fit the parallelogram (relation as vector) model more closely; humans lean on accessible words.
numbers: Preregistered; reuses Peterson, Chen, Griffiths (2020) problems. Effect sizes not extracted (abstract and introduction read).
limits: Abstract-level only.
agent_relevance: LLMs apply one relation consistently across pairs more reliably than people.

source: Sourati, Ilievski, Sommerauer, Jiang (2024) ARN: Analogical Reasoning on Narratives
finding: Narrative analogies with surface vs system (relational) mappings. Models spot near analogies but fail far ones; GPT-4 zero-shot is below random on (far,near).
limits: Binary task. Few-shot and CoT help but best model stays about halfway between random and human.
agent_relevance: Surface similarity beats relational structure in far cases: ask for the abstract message before comparing.

source: Sourati et al. (2024) ARN: effect of distractor elements
finding: Action-based surface mappings were the most distracting; combined surface distractors hurt more than any single element.
numbers: UnifiedQA-11B reached 74.6% on (far,near), beating GPT models, and did better with all distractor types included.
limits: Odd UnifiedQA result unexplained.
agent_relevance: Strip surface cues (names, actions) when comparing structures.

source: Lampinen et al. (2024) Language models show human-like content effects on reasoning tasks
finding: Models, like people, reason better when meaning supports the logic and worse when it conflicts, across NLI, syllogisms and Wason.
numbers: Numbers are in figures; only abstract and text claims read.
limits: Not a relation-label manipulation.
agent_relevance: Content-free relation labels may help or hurt: test both.

source: Gendron et al. (2024) Large language models are not strong abstract reasoners
finding: LLMs perform poorly on text versions of abstract tasks (ACRE, RAVEN text); in-context examples and fine-tuning help; encoding choice changes results.
numbers: Accuracy rises with number of in-context examples, up to about 0.6 at 16 examples for Text-Davinci-3 and GPT-4 on some tasks.
limits: Limited extraction.
agent_relevance: Text encoding choice changes results: choose names deliberately.

source: Christie & Gentner (2014) Language helps children succeed on a classic analogy task
finding: Cited by Hu et al.: giving even nonsense names to relations improves children's relational reasoning.
numbers: Not read by me; no numbers recorded.
limits: Secondhand via the Hu et al. text only.
agent_relevance: Human source for the S2 naming idea.

source: Gentner et al. (2013) deaf children without spatial relational language in sign
finding: Cited by Hu et al.: deaf children whose sign language lacks spatial relations did worse than hearing children on a spatial relational task.
numbers: Not read; no numbers.
limits: Secondhand.
agent_relevance: Language supplies the relational vocabulary the task needs.

source: Gap note: Lupyan label effects and LLMs
finding: Search found no paper that tests Lupyan's label-feedback or Gentner's relational-label effect on LLMs directly; Hu et al. 2023 is the closest.
numbers: 0 direct LLM tests of label-induced relational comparison found in this session.
limits: Search limited: 2 of 6 WebSearch used, OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar quotas exhausted, arXiv API rate limited.
agent_relevance: Open gap: a clean test of relation names in agent prompts is cheap to run.

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2023) semantic distance effect in verbal analogies
finding: On the Jones et al. verbal analogy set GPT-3 did worse when the A-B and C-D pairs came from semantically distant domains, as people do.
numbers: Human N=241 in the Jones et al. set; GPT-3 numerically weaker than humans there; exact per-condition values are in Figure 7d, not extracted.
limits: Figure-only numbers; GPT-3 only.
agent_relevance: Far-domain relation mapping is the weak spot; S2 should name the relation in domain-free words before comparing.
